Alabama.ag_notification_note: Only if more than 1,000 Alabama residents must be notified — then the company must also tell the Attorney General and the consumer reporting agencies within 45 days.
Alabama.agency_name: Office of the Attorney General of Alabama
Alabama.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, so set one up with each bureau if your information was exposed.
Alabama.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out as fast as possible and without unreasonable delay, and no later than 45 days after the company determines a breach happened that is reasonably likely to cause substantial harm. Law enforcement can ask for a delay if notice would interfere with a criminal investigation.
Alabama.private_right_note: No — only the Attorney General can enforce the law, including civil penalties of up to $5,000 per day, capped at $500,000 per breach. You cannot sue under this statute.
Alabama.state_note: Alabama's law is harm-based: if the company investigates and documents that harm is not reasonably likely, it may skip notifying you — but it must first send that written determination to the Attorney General.
Alabama.statute_name: Alabama Data Breach Notification Act of 2018

Alaska.ag_notification_note: No. Alaska does not require the company to notify the Attorney General about a breach. If more than 1,000 residents are affected, the company must notify the nationwide credit bureaus instead. The AG only gets a written notice if the company claims no harm is likely and skips notifying you.
Alaska.agency_name: Alaska Department of Law, Office of the Attorney General
Alaska.freeze_rights_note: Alaska's own freeze law sits in the same act, and federal law makes freezes free: you can freeze your credit file with each of the three bureaus at no cost and lift it for free when you apply for credit.
Alaska.notification_deadline_note: The law sets no number of days. The company must tell you in the most expeditious time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to figure out the scope of the breach and fix the system. Police can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation.
Alaska.private_right_note: Limited. A violation counts as an unfair or deceptive trade practice, and you can seek your actual economic damages, capped at $500. The state can also fine the company up to $500 per resident not notified, capped at $50,000.
Alaska.state_note: Alaska has no fixed deadline in days and no duty to tell the Attorney General, so if you hear nothing, check your credit reports and consider a freeze rather than waiting for an official notice.

Arizona.ag_notification_note: Only if the breach requires notifying more than 1,000 people — then the company must also notify the Attorney General and the director of the Arizona Department of Homeland Security in writing, within the same 45 days.
Arizona.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
Arizona.notification_deadline_note: The clock starts when the company's investigation determines a breach occurred. Notice must be made in the most expedient manner possible and without unreasonable delay, and in any case within 45 days after that determination. Law enforcement can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation.
Arizona.private_right_note: No. The statute says only the Attorney General may enforce it, with civil penalties up to $500,000 per breach. You cannot sue under this statute.
Arizona.state_note: Arizona is unusual in also requiring notice to the state homeland security director for big breaches, and the breach notice itself must include the toll-free numbers for the three credit bureaus and the FTC.

Arkansas.ag_notification_note: Only if the breach affects the personal information of more than 1,000 individuals — then the company must tell the Attorney General at the same time it notifies you, or within 45 days after determining harm is reasonably likely, whichever comes first.
Arkansas.agency_name: Office of the Arkansas Attorney General
Arkansas.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
Arkansas.notification_deadline_note: Arkansas sets no number of days. The company must tell you in the most expedient time and manner possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. No notice is needed at all if the company determines after investigation that there is no reasonable likelihood of harm.
Arkansas.private_right_note: No. Violations are enforced only by the Attorney General under the Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The statute gives individuals no right to sue.
Arkansas.state_note: Arkansas has no fixed number of days for notifying you, and notice can be skipped entirely if the company decides harm is not reasonably likely — so watch your accounts and credit reports yourself.

California.ag_notification_note: If more than 500 California residents must be notified from a single breach, the company must electronically send a sample copy of the notice to the Attorney General within 15 calendar days after notifying consumers. The Attorney General publishes these notices.
California.agency_name: California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General
California.freeze_rights_note: Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus, and California law also gives you a free freeze right. A freeze is the strongest step you can take — it stops new accounts from being opened in your name.
California.notification_deadline_note: Since January 1, 2026, notice must go out within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the breach, with delays allowed only for law enforcement needs or to determine the scope and restore the system. The notice must be in plain language, titled 'Notice of Data Breach,' with set headings.
California.private_right_note: Limited but real. Under the CCPA (Civil Code § 1798.150), you can sue if your unencrypted personal information was accessed and stolen or disclosed because the business failed to use reasonable security — for $100 to $750 per consumer per incident or your actual damages, whichever is greater. For statutory damages you must first give the business 30 days' written notice and a chance to cure.
California.state_note: California is the strongest of these ten states: a 30-day deadline, a sample notice to the Attorney General for breaches over 500 people, and a required offer of at least 12 months of free identity-theft prevention services if your Social Security or driver's license number was exposed and the company was the source of the breach. Note the Legal Aid Association of California is a statewide association, not a law firm — it points you to your local legal aid office.

Colorado.ag_notification_note: If the breach is reasonably believed to have affected 500 or more Colorado residents, the company must also notify the Attorney General within 30 days of determining the breach occurred.
Colorado.agency_name: Colorado Attorney General's Office (Colorado Department of Law)
Colorado.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
Colorado.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 30 days after the company determines a breach occurred. Law enforcement can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation.
Colorado.private_right_note: No. The Attorney General enforces the law and can sue for compliance or direct economic damages. The statute creates no private right for consumers.
Colorado.state_note: Colorado's 30-day deadline is one of the shortest in the country, and the breach notice must include the toll-free numbers for the credit bureaus and the FTC plus a statement about fraud alerts and security freezes.

Connecticut.ag_notification_note: Yes — for every breach, with no minimum number of people. The company must notify the Attorney General no later than the time it notifies affected residents.
Connecticut.agency_name: Connecticut Office of the Attorney General
Connecticut.freeze_rights_note: Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus. Connecticut's breach notice must also tell you how to place a freeze on your credit file.
Connecticut.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery of the breach, unless a shorter time is required under federal law. If more affected residents turn up after 60 days, the company must still notify them as quickly as possible. No notice is needed if the company reasonably determines the breach will not likely cause harm.
Connecticut.private_right_note: No. A violation is treated as an unfair trade practice, but enforcement is by the Attorney General only — the statute creates no private right for consumers.
Connecticut.state_note: Connecticut is one of only three states in this set that require free identity-theft help: if your Social Security number was involved, the company must offer you at least 24 months of free identity-theft prevention and mitigation services, and the Attorney General must be told about every breach, not just big ones.
Connecticut.statute_name: Breach of Security Involving Computerized Data Containing Personal Information

Delaware.ag_notification_note: Only if more than 500 Delaware residents must be notified — then the company must tell the Attorney General no later than the time it notifies residents.
Delaware.agency_name: Delaware Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General
Delaware.freeze_rights_note: Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus, and Delaware's own law requires the breach notice to include information on how to place a freeze on your credit file.
Delaware.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be made without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after the company determines a breach occurred, unless federal law requires a shorter time or law enforcement asks for a delay. No notice is needed if the company reasonably determines the breach is unlikely to harm you.
Delaware.private_right_note: No. The 2017 amendment removed the private right the original 2005 law had. Only the Attorney General can bring an action under this chapter, including to recover direct economic damages.
Delaware.state_note: If your Social Security number was in the breach, Delaware requires the company to offer you one year of free credit monitoring and to explain how to freeze your credit — take them up on both.

Florida.ag_notification_note: Yes — the notice goes to the Department of Legal Affairs (the Attorney General's office). Any breach affecting 500 or more Floridians must be reported to the Department within 30 days, and even a 'no harm' determination must be sent to the Department within 30 days.
Florida.agency_name: Florida Attorney General, Department of Legal Affairs
Florida.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
Florida.notification_deadline_note: Notice to you must go out as expeditiously as practicable and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 30 days after the company determines a breach occurred or has reason to believe one did. Law enforcement can delay notice during a criminal investigation, and the company can get 15 extra days if it shows good cause in writing to the Department.
Florida.private_right_note: No. The statute says so directly: it does not establish a private cause of action. Only the Department can enforce it, with civil penalties up to $500,000 per breach.
Florida.state_note: Florida has one of the tightest deadlines (30 days) and makes the company report to the state even when it claims no harm will result — if you get a breach letter, check whether the company offered any free services, because Florida does not require it to.

Georgia.ag_notification_note: No. The notification statute never names the Attorney General, so a private company has no duty to tell the AG about a breach. If more than 10,000 Georgia residents must be notified at once, the company must instead notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
Georgia.agency_name: Georgia Department of Law, Office of the Attorney General
Georgia.freeze_rights_note: Georgia has its own freeze law, and federal law makes freezes free at all three bureaus — place one if your Social Security or driver's license number was exposed.
Georgia.notification_deadline_note: Georgia sets no number of days. The company must notify you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. Law enforcement can delay notice during a criminal investigation.
Georgia.private_right_note: No. The Personal Identity Protection Act gives you no right to sue under it; the Attorney General enforces violations as unfair practices under the Fair Business Practices Act. You may still have claims under other laws, such as negligence.
Georgia.state_note: Georgia is the weakest timeline in this set: no deadline in days, no notice to the Attorney General, and no required credit monitoring — so act on your own fast: freeze your credit and watch your accounts yourself.
